newsitem.title: JAPAN: Okinawa base could cause Japan-US rift, PM warns.
newsitem.headline: Okinawa base could cause Japan-US rift, PM warns.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto warned on Monday that a dispute between the central government and Okinawa landowners over leases for U.S. military bases could cause a rift in Japan-U.S. ties.
Forced leases for land on the southern island of Okinawa occupied by 12 U.S. military facilities and owned by landlords who oppose the U.S. presence expire on May 14.

A special Okinawa prefecture committee expected to rule on the forced leases begins hearings on February 21 and is unlikely to deliver a verdict before the May 14 lapse of the leases, Hashimoto told a parliamentary committee.

"If a situation develops in which we are unable (to procure the land), it could cause a rift in Japan-U.S. relations," Hashimoto said in response to general policy questions by the opposition at parliament's lower house budget committee.

Hashimoto last year resolved a similar lease dispute by obtaining Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota's cooperation in renewing land contracts in exchange for a sweeping plan to cut the concentration of U.S. bases and promote economic development on the tiny island.

Those measures and other steps to phase out U.S. bases, however, have only taken Hashimoto "30 percent down the road to a solution to the Okinawa problem", the prime minister's special adviser on Okinawa told reporters.

Yukio Okamoto, a former senior diplomat, said that a hardline government reply -- such as parliament drafting a special bill to allow confiscation of the land, risks "igniting a firestorm of controversy".
According to media reports, the government is considering a two-phase policy to avoid what after May 14 would be a de facto illegal occupation of the Okinawans land by U.S. forces.

The first step would be for the government to file a request to the special Okinawa prefecture committee for an emergency six-month permit to use the land, owned by 3,000 landowners opposed to the U.S. presence, media reports said.
The second step would involve steps to revise the law under which the government can force landowners to lease land to the state to allow continued use of the 12 facilities, the reports said.
Okinawa Governor Ota, who is slated to meet Hashimoto in Tokyo later this month, on Monday criticised the government's approach.
Ota also reiterated his refusal to get involved in Tokyo's efforts to pursuade the Okinawan city of Nago to accept feasibility studies for an offshore helicopter port.

Last April Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton agreed to relocate the helicopter port from the crowded city of Futenma, where neighbours feared accidents and resented the noise, to another site.
Okinawan antipathy to the U.S. bases, which occupy about one-fifth of the land of the sub-tropical island, exploded in September 1995 after the rape of a local schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.
The three are serving prison sentences for the crime.
